articles.title: A broken power accord
articles.content: ALTHOUGH the PTI haspostponedits protest march on Islamabad, the capital city’s container-blocked roads continue to reflect the country’s deeper crisis. The crisis is not merely political, economic, or security-related; it is rooted in an elite class that cannot forge an accord within themselves. Islamabad is not witnessing a siege-like situation for the first time; it has become part of life for the inhabitants of the twin cities. Even a cricket match or a visiting dignitary can bring life to a standstill. Despite huge investments in infrastructure and expensive surveillance systems, the security providers remain nervous. They have turned the federal capital into a city of checkpoints, where the average citizen must pass through long queues every 10 minutes during his daily commute — with police officers regarding him with suspicious eyes. Citizens end up feeling that they themselves are responsible for all the country’s ills, while those who have actually encroached on green belts, footpaths, and even highways escape punishment for crimes they do not even understand. The crisis runs deep, and even the postponement of the protest by the PTI, and earlier by theJamaat-i-Islami, will not solve the country’s political, governance, economic, and security crisis. These lines may seem cynical, but the streets of the federal capital tell Pakistan’s whole story. The ‘container-ment’ approach shows serious fractures among the power elites over the division of power, which has not been shared proportionately and has, in fact, caused a chronic political crisis and led to a rent-seeking economy. Rent-seeking means economic actors become adept at obtaining privileged access to the state or controlling scarce resources. The masses are not responsible for the country’s state of affairs; it is fractured power elites who have yet to learn the art of distributing power among themselves. Here, another term needs explaining. The ‘fractured elite’ comprises Pakistan’s dominant political, civil-military, judicial, and institutional elite — sometimes referred to as the establishment — when it no longer agrees on the basic rules of the political game. The elite includes religious and ideological authorities, but in an evolving power order, their role and share have been minimised for now. Major businesses and landed interests have become important actors within the fractured power order. Serious fractures exist among the elites over the division of power. A question arises: what does an elite power accord look like? Is it about who will have the political power to govern, and under what conditions? Another question emerges: aside from political power, who holds the real power, also referred to as institutional power? Does this authority belong to parliament, the executive, the military, the judiciary, or the bureaucracy? Institutional power brings control over major economic resources and rents, as well as coercive or security institutions. It also has territorial power to determine how the interests of the centre and the provinces are accommodated. Among the elites, succession remains a key question: how will power change hands? A linked challenge arises. How are influential groups accommodated? Foreign policy remains the exclusive domain of the power elites — what strategic interests are considered non-negotiable? Now look at the Pakistani elites, which have failed to define the role of political power. Gradually, an institution has assumed authority, while the ruling political parties have surrendered several rights to retain power. The opposition, meanwhile, is demanding its legitimate rights. Many political analysts arguably contend that the opposition, now led by the PTI, along with smaller parties within the opposition alliance, the Tehreek-i-Tahaffuz-i-Ayeen-i-Pakistan, is struggling for power rather than restoring or developing a new social contract in the country. Maulana Fazlur Rahman’s JUI-F is also part of the opposition. It has been marginalised in the power structure because the changing rules in the power playbook leave less space for religious actors now. The political power structure has clearly failed to advance nationhood, and power remains confined to one major influential ethnic group in the country. Those who represent the power structure in the public discourse and the social and mainstream media malign less powerful and marginalised groups, suggesting they go to Afghanistan — their remarks target both the Pakhtuns and the Baloch. They stigmatise the Kashmiris as well, who have been demanding their rights in Azad Kashmir. If state propagandists are suggesting a course of action for them, where are they supposed to go? Fractured power elites cannot create cohesion within a nation. They cannot resolve their internal discord, so how can they devise a broad formula for national cohesion? In their paranoid view, security has taken over dialogue, and they have grown accustomed to killing an ant with a hammer. Even when clear indications show dialogue is the best policy, power elites know it would mean accommodating new members in the power club and remain hesitant to admit newcomers. A lack of flexibility or capacity for dialogue creates a need for a hyper-coercive internal security order. An internal security review is underway to make it more coercive. KP has resisted somewhat by introducing thePolice Act, 2026,which will bring provincial government oversight over the system, as was required in the KP context, where discord between the police and other institutions has become challenging. But the federal government is resisting it. It seems the power elites will not compromise on the new internal security order and will continue to push their agenda through Nacta or the interior ministry. Foreign policy and geopolitics are sensitive domains for public discourse in the country. The parameters of non-negotiable interests continue to blur and narrow. For the masses, the crisis in the country is no more than a long, tragic soap opera on screen, which they can watch, cry over, and laugh at, but cannot act on.
articles.author: Muhammad Amir Rana

articles.title: The Houthi blockade
articles.content: IN July 2026, the Houthisdeclareda naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, targeting Saudi-linked shipping, and warning commercial vessels of any nationality against calling at Saudi ports. Vessels deemed to breach the blockade faced attack wherever they entered the Houthis’ operational reach. Attacks on Saudi tankers and energy infrastructure were followed by traffic through Bab al-Mandeb falling to its lowest level in months. By September, Houthi forces hadseizedstrategic islands around Bab al-Mandeb and gained control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, increasing their capacity to threaten, disrupt and potentially control maritime traffic through the strait. The conventional legal position is that naval blockade is a belligerent right associated with international armed conflict (IAC), mainly because it permits interference with neutral commercial shipping. As per this view, a non-state armed group engaged solely in a non-international armed conflict does not ordinarily have the authority to impose a blockade that is binding on neutral vessels. However, customary international law does not conclusively foreclose blockade in a sufficiently intense NIAC, particularly where an organised armed group exercises extensive territorial and governmental control and can enforce maritime restrictions. This question is particularly significant in Yemen, where there is a strong argument that the Houthis function as a de facto governmental authority rather than merely an insurgent movement. They have long controlled Sana’a, govern territory containing a substantial population, and have expanded along the Red Sea coast and around Bab al-Mandeb. Crucially, under the ICRC approach, effective governmental control, rather than global recognition alone, is central to determining de facto governmental authority. If the Houthis are treated as exercising Yemen’s governmental authority, their external hostilities may be characterised as those of Yemen itself, strengthening the argument that the relevant conflicts are international and that traditional belligerent rights, including blockade, are potentially available. Even if this characterisation is rejected, other factors point towards possible internationalisation. Saudi Arabia is directly engaged alongside the internationally recognised Yemeni authorities against the Houthis, while the latter have repeatedly attacked Saudi territory. Saudi intervention by invitation does not, by itself, transform the underlying conflict into an IAC, but it adds an international dimension. Israel provides a separate route: it has used force on Yemeni territory in response to Houthi attacks, and under the ICRC’s view, the unconsented use of force by one state against another state’s territory may itself create an IAC between them, even where the immediate target is a non-state armed group. Israeli strikes on Houthi-held territory could therefore support a parallel Israel-Yemen IAC. Do the Houthis, as a non-state armed group, have the legal authority to enforce a naval blockade? Iranian involvement provides another possible route to internationalisation. Arms, financing and political support alone are insufficient. Under the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia’s “overall control” test in Tadić, however, the threshold may be met where a state, beyond financing, training or equipping an organised armed group, also participates in planning its military activities; specific instructions for each operation are unnecessary. The ICJ’s stricter “effective control” test, relevant to attribution of particular conduct, requires proof that the state directed or controlled the specific operation in question. Accordingly, if the conflict is international, traditional blockade law is more readily applicable; if the Houthis remain solely a non-state party to an NIAC, their authority to impose blockade obligations on neutral shipping remains controversial. In either case, a declaration alone is insufficient: a blockade must satisfy the requirements of effectiveness, notification, impartiality and applicable humanitarian limitations. Regardless of classification, the Houthis are bound by applicable international humanitarian law. In an NIAC, Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and applicable customary IHL apply; in an IAC, the Geneva Conventions apply in full, together with customary IHL. In either case, rules governing distinction, military goals, proportionality and precautions constrain the conduct of hostilities. The law of naval blockade is further governed by the law of armed conflict at sea and customary international law, as elaborated in the San Remo Manual. Under paragraphs 93-104, a blockade must be declared and notified to belligerents and neutral states; specify its commencement, duration, location and extent; allow neutral vessels an appropriate period to depart; be effective and impartially applied; and comply with humanitarian restrictions, including those concerning essential civilian supplies. Importantly, the Houthis have denied seeking to close Bab al-Mandeb to international navigation. Their spokesman stated that there was “no closure” of the strait and described the measure as a maritime blockade affecting only the Saudi side. The main legal question, therefore, is not whether the Houthis may close Bab al-Mandeb as a coastal authority, but whether they may lawfully impose and enforce a belligerent blockade against Saudi Arabia and shipping falling within its scope. Military necessity, however, does not independently make commercial shipping a lawful target. Article 52(2) of Additional Protocol I, reflecting the customary definition of a military objective, requires an object, by its nature, location, purpose or use, to make an effective contribution to military action and for its destruction, capture or neutralisation to offer a definite military advantage. Particular Saudi vessels, ports or assets directly supporting military operations may satisfy that test, but the general contribution of commercial trade to Saudi Arabia’s economy and war capacity does not, by itself, transform every merchant vessel into a military goal. Any attack remains subject to distinction, proportionality and precautions. This distinction is particularly important for neutral shipping. Neutral vessels do not lose protection merely because they trade with Saudi Arabia or indirectly contribute to its economy. Whether a vessel may lawfully be intercepted, captured or attacked must be determined under the specific rules governing blockade, neutral shipping and military objectives, rather than through a general invocation of military necessity. Finally, the simultaneous closure of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb would place roughly a quarter of global oil flows and a major share of LNG trade at risk. Some analysts view pressure on both chokepoints as part of a broader Iranian strategy, working through the Houthis to increase economic pressure on the US and its Gulf partners and create leverage over the wider war. Pakistan hascondemnedHouthi attacks on Saudi Arabia while continuing to stress diplomacy and regional de-escalation. It has so far avoided direct military involvement under the Makkah accord, maintaining a cautious approach that limits the risk of Pakistan being drawn into the widening regional conflict. The writer is a professor of law at Lums.
articles.author: Sikander Ahmed Shah

articles.title: Hope, not heroes
articles.content: MY sisters insisted I watch Project Hail Mary. It was, they said, exactly the right film for dispiriting times. I finally watched it on the long flight home and they were right. The title refers to the Hail Mary pass, the desperate last throw in American football when nothing else is left. The phrase itself comes from a prayer to Mary, or Maryam as we refer to her here, a plea to be rescued from above. The film’s hero is a schoolteacher who wakes up alone in space, with no memory of how he got there and no great enthusiasm for dying to save the planet. He is not a soldier, a politician or a billionaire. He is frightened. He makes mistakes. He improvises. He does what ordinary people do when faced with an extraordinary problem: he deals with whatever is in front of him and hopes the next thing will be manageable. Then he meets Rocky, an alien. At first they cannot even communicate. They have a different biology, different languages and different reasons for being where they are. Yet the heart of the film is not the rescue of Earth. It is two very different beings learning to trust each other. The world is not saved by one exceptional person. It is saved by cooperation. Pakistan can feel like a place designed to exhaust hope. I landed to find another flight was still dominating the news. Punjab’s chief minister, Maryam Nawaz, had used the provincial government’s aircraft to attend her daughter’s graduation in London. Faced with criticism, she said she had paid Rs27.5 million for the trip from her own pocket, that the plane belonged to the Chief Minister Office rather than to her, and that all four provincial chief ministers had one. She was not accountable, she said, to vloggers and YouTubers, but to God and the people. She may well have paid. That is not really the point. What struck me was how she defended it. The plane, she said, belongs to the office, not to her. A chief minister’s time is valuable. Her critics are not really upset about the plane but about her work. All these arguments come down to the same idea: that she matters so much that making her journey easier is somehow a favour to the rest of us. I suppose we too are meant to pray for a miracle. Many of us do, for someone else. At the moment, probably Imran Khan. His time in government was hardly a lesson in how to run a country. Yet even in custody he carries the hopes of millions who believe that, given one more chance, he alone could set everything right. We are practised at this kind of hope. We look upward: to the prime minister, the chief minister, the general, the billionaire, the technocrat, the great leader who will finally arrive and sort everything out. The supporters of each believe their saviour is different. The critics of each are already waiting for the next one. It is not hard to see why. Pakistan can feel like a place designed to exhaust hope. There is always another political quarrel, economic worry or institutional failure waiting to consume the day. We watch the powerful fight over who controls the machinery while the rest of us wonder whether the machinery works at all. Project Hail Mary offers a different fantasy. Not that a great person will save us, but that people will help one another. Its act of faith is not in human exceptionalism but in human usefulness. You don’t have to be extraordinary to matter. You don’t have to have the answers. You don’t even have to understand the person beside you. You only have to keep working on the problem together. We have seen this at home. When a cable car snapped over a ravine in Battagram in 2023, leaving eight people hanging for 14 hours, it was local men who understood those wires, rigging a line in the dark, who brought them back. Nobody waited for a saviour. There wasn’t time. They worked with the police and the military. None of this means leaders don’t matter. Governments, institutions and competence matter, and people with power carry responsibilities that ordinary citizens do not. That is precisely why it matters how they travel, and whom they believe they are serving. But no chief minister, prime minister or political dynasty can substitute for the millions of small acts of competence, decency and courage that keep a society running. Ryland Grace does not save the world by becoming a messiah. He saves it by becoming useful. Perhaps that is the hope we could use here. Not that a hero is coming, on a government jet or otherwise, but that there are still people willing to look at the next impossible problem and say: all right, let’s figure this out. The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: War in the Gulf
articles.content: THE war that the US and Israel imposed on Iran this year has failed to achieve any of the objectives that the two countries had intended. The declared purpose was to prevent Iran from building a nuclear weapon. A fact-check indicates that Iran had kept its civil nuclear programme under IAEA safeguards. It had also willingly agreed to a nuclear deal in 2015. It was President Donald Trump who pulled the US out of the deal in 2018 and re-engaged with Iran in his second term under a “maximum pressure” campaign. While talks were still underway, Israel attacked Iran in June 2025, resulting in a 12-day war. Having failed to subdue Iran, the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran on Feb 28, this year, killing much of the Iranian leadership and relentlessly bombing Iranian facilities and installations for 40 days. All this while Iran remained in the NPT and maintained that it was not building a nuclear bomb, thanks in large measure to a directive from Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei to not pursue a nuclear weapon programme. This means that Tehran’s nuclear programme was only a pretext to attack Iran this year. Arguably, the real objective of the February strike was to change the ruling regime in Iran. It would be recalled that by 2020, many Arab countries had joined the Abraham Accords and normalised relations with Israel. Lest the Palestinian cause be forgotten, Hamas mounted a resistance attack on Israel in October 2023, which was used by the Benjamin Netanyahu government to bomb Gaza to rubble, committing horrific genocide. Having weakened Hamas and Hezbollah, Israel began to entertain the idea of establishing a ‘Greater Israel’ and found the Iranian regime to be a major roadblock to its ambitions. Since his efforts to dislodge Iran’s government had failed in June 2025, Netanyahu persuaded Trump to undertake a joint attack against Iran on Feb 28. Two factors seem to have encouraged Trump to accept this gamble. He had successfully dislodged the government of president Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela in January, and Iran had witnessed massive protests against the government on account of inflation. The US and Israeli leadership wrongly assessed that they would be able to wipe out the Iranian regime within days. They also failed to destroy Iran’s long-range missile programme, though they did succeed in weakening Iran’s Axis of Resistance. The conflict has been nothing short of a disaster for the US itself. While Iran has survived the American and Israeli onslaught, the war has been nothing less than a disaster for the US itself. For the first time, there is a fracture in America’s relations with the Jewish state. The Gulf states are increasingly becoming disillusioned with America’s capacity or will to provide them with security. The US bases in the region have been practically destroyed. The myth of invincibility of the US military machine has been shattered. The Strait of Hormuz, which was open before the war, is now being contested. The war is expanding horizontally, with Iraqi militias targeting Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline and Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi cities and oil installations. Bab al-Mandeb also runs the risk of closure as the Houthis have captured all key positions and islands along the Red Sea. With oil prices soaring, most countries have run into serious economic difficulties. The Gulf countries, whose economies largely depended on energy flows, tourism, and services, have been shaken to the core. Meanwhile, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye have entered into a regional arrangement for joint defence, predicated on the principle of collective security. With Israeli parliamentary elections due on Oct 27 and mid-term Congressional elections in America on Nov 3, the US is contemplating how best to handle the war with Iran. One way is to revert to the MoU that was mediated by Pakistan and signed in June by the presidents of the US and Iran. However, the MoU had received severe criticism within the US and was largely interpreted as capitulation by the US. Ever since, Trump has pulled back from any peace attempts. The other option being considered is to resort to another large-scale military attack. Given what had happened in the earlier military campaigns, it can be safely assumed that another confrontation is unlikely to yield a different result. The only feasible solution is diplomacy. Pakistan, Qatar, and others must continue their efforts for peace. Secondly, it is time for China to step in as a mediator as it depends heavily on oil flows from the Gulf and had successfully brokered normalisation between Iran and Saudi Arabia in 2023. China should also impress upon the US leadership the futility of finding a military solution to the crisis in the Gulf region. The writer is chairman Sanober Institute and a former foreign secretary of Pakistan.
articles.author: Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry

articles.title: Balochistan’s reality
articles.content: IF the state is to bring peace to Balochistan, then its representatives must face the ground realities. However, holders of high office at times almost trivialise the province’s problems. For example, at an event in Quetta recently, Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti said there was no insurgency in the province, but that some elements were promoting separatist ideas. He added that it was incorrect to attribute unrest in Balochistan to lack of development. Mr Bugti asked the youth to distinguish between “facts and perceptions”. Not long after his remarks, the military said it had killed at least 33 terrorists over the past few days in the province. Mr Bugti’s comments are similar to those made by the federal interior minister some years back, when he said Balochistan’s terrorism problem could be handled by a station house officer. Many moons after those words, Balochistan continues to suffer from frequent terrorist attacks. As per one count, there were at least 89 terrorist attacks in Balochistan in August. At times, major highways in the province are cut off by violent elements, while the provincial government has had to place curbs on nighttime travel. Terrorists have stormed towns, and in July, the nation’s top civilian and military leadership rushed to Quetta to take stock of the situation. All these events, taken together, point to a terrorist insurgency, and it would be ill-advised for the state to underplay what is going on in the province. Mr Bugti also said that unrest and backwardness in the province were not linked. This observation is incorrect. The fact is that the province has the poorest socioeconomic indicators in Pakistan, and terrorists exploit this situation to gain recruits and swell their ranks. The need, therefore, is for the state to honestly appraise the situation in Balochistan. Handling the issue involves both kinetic measures to eliminate violent elements — who may be supported by hostile states — and engagement with groups that reject violence and opt for dialogue. But the initial step requires officials to accept the nature and scope of the problem. Balochistan’s people must live in an atmosphere free of terrorism and enjoy a major share of the province’s natural wealth. This goal can only be achieved when the state honestly diagnoses the province’s problems and sincerely strives to address them.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Progress at UNGA
articles.content: ALTHOUGH no breakthrough was achieved at the UN General Assembly, there has been some progress where finding a negotiated solution to the US war on Iran is concerned. For example, both the American and Iranian delegations heldtalksmediated by Qatar, while the Iranian presidenttoldPrime Minister Shehbaz Sharif that Tehran was still committed to the Islamabad MoU. Moreover, other reports indicate that both the US and Iran are looking for an off-ramp, with Tehran offering to open the Strait of Hormuz for marine traffic if Washington ends its blockade of Iran. The key question is: who will blink first in this battle of wits, as neither side will want to appear weak? Now it is up to both sides — as well as the states mediating this conflict — to take forward the progress made in New York. As the US, along with Israel, initiated this aggression, it should take the first step and offer confidence-building measures to Iran in order to de-escalate the situation and come to a long-term settlement. Though White House officials have said Iran is ‘desperate’ for a deal, the fact is that high fuel prices are also hurting the Trump administration at home. An unpopular war coupled with high inflation is not likely to have a positive effect on the Republicans’ chances going into November’s midterm elections. In a meeting on the UNGA sidelines, Mr Trump’s Gulf allies reportedly asked him for a post-midterm strategy regarding Iran. Perhaps something can come out of the interactions at the UN. However, the talks must not be a ruse to open Hormuz and to merely suspend hostilities and stabilise oil prices until the US midterms. There are some indications that the Trump administration may be considering kinetic action after the elections. It would mean a disastrous new confrontation in the Middle East. Hopefully, wiser counsel will prevail in Washington. The way forward seems simple. The US must approach Iran with sincerity, and the talks must not be a smokescreen for further military action later. The blockade of Iran should be lifted and its funds released to enable a longer-term peace. Tehran, on its part, should commit to keeping Hormuz open in the interest of both its neighbours and the wider international community, while also refraining from targeting the Gulf states. Also, any new agreement should cover all fronts: Gaza, Lebanon and Yemen. Although these are separate conflicts, they are also interlinked as Iranian allies are involved in all of them fighting Israel, the US and Saudi Arabia. Hence, a peace treaty with Iran alone may not last unless there is also calm in other regional theatres, while there is a particular need to rein in Israel’s murderous attacks on regional states.
articles.author: Editorial
